turns.text: True, I never thought of it like that.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Short breaks actually help your focus. Your brain needs a reset every hour or so.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What should I even do in a five minute break?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Get away from screens. Stretch, step outside, make tea, look out of the window.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Not scroll my phone, then.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ideally not. It feels like a break, but your eyes and brain are still working.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. I'll try the tea / and window thing this afternoon.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good plan. Notice how you feel at four o'clock, that's usually when it shows.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My internet keeps dropping during video calls. Any quick fixes?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: First, try moving closer to the router, or plug in with a cable if you can. Wifi through walls loses a lot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The router's two floors down.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then a wifi extender or a mesh system could help. Also check whether anyone at home is streaming or downloading during your calls.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My son plays online games all afternoon.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That might be it. Many routers let you prioritize your work laptop, look for a setting called quality of service.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Sounds technical, / but I'll give it a go.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's usually just a couple of clicks in the router app. And in a pinch, turning off your camera saves a lot of bandwidth.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it okay to work from my bed sometimes?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Once in a while is fine, but doing it often can hurt your sleep. Your brain starts linking the bed with work.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh no, I do it pretty much daily.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then try a small change, like working from the sofa or a kitchen chair, even with the same laptop.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: But my bed is so comfy.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I get it. A lap desk at least keeps your neck in a better position, if you do stay there.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about my back?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pillows behind you so you're not hunched over. But honestly, a proper chair will feel better by the end of the day.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can you help me plan my day? I've got a report, three calls and a pile of emails.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sure. When are the calls?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ten, two and half past four.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then do the report first thing, before ten, while your head is fresh. That's your deep work block.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And the emails?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Clear them in two short bursts, maybe right after lunch and after the last call. Don't keep the inbox open while you write.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's hard for me, / I check it constantly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Close the tab completely and turn off the notifications for the morning. If something's urgent, people will call.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'm doing it. Report first.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Great. Take a short walk before the two o'clock call, it'll help you reset.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My eyes feel tired after a day at the screen. Is that normal?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Very normal. Try the twenty twenty twenty rule, every twenty minutes look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's a lot of twenties.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's easy to remember, at least. Also check your screen brightness, it should roughly match the room.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mine is probably way too bright.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a common cause. And make sure you blink, people blink much less while staring at screens.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I get those blue light glasses?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The evidence for them is mixed. Breaks and better lighting usually help more. If it keeps up, see an optician.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it weird to get dressed properly when working from home?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not weird at all. Lots of people find it helps them switch into work mode.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've been in pajamas for a week, honestly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No judgment, but you might notice a difference. Even jeans and a nice top can change how you feel.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about shoes? / That seems a bit much.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some people swear by it. Shoes signal that you're at work, then taking them off marks the end of the day.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Huh, kind of like a uniform.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. Small rituals like that help your brain separate home time from work time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I tell my family I need to not be interrupted while working?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Be clear and specific. Instead of I'm busy, try, from nine to twelve I'm working, please only knock if it's urgent.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My youngest is six. She doesn't care about schedules.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For kids, a visual signal helps. A sign on the door, red for do not disturb and green for come in.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, she'd love making that sign.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Even better, let her make it. Kids respect rules they helped create.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And my partner?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Share your calendar, and agree on a quick way to check in, like a text instead of walking in mid call.

option_sets.lead_in: I need help deciding where to set up my home office.
options: The first option is the spare bedroom, which has a door but is pretty small and dark.
Then there's a corner of the living room, lots of light, but my kids play there all afternoon.
And the last choice is the basement, quiet and roomy, but there's no window at all.
moshi_comment: With kids playing in the living room, that corner would be tough for calls and focus. The spare bedroom has the big advantage of a door, and a good lamp can fix the darkness. How often are you on video calls?
The basement is the quietest and most spacious, but working all day without daylight can really drag you down. I'd go with the spare bedroom and add some bright warm lighting.

option_sets.lead_in: My company gave me five hundred dollars for my home office, and I'm stuck on how to spend it.
options: One option is a really good ergonomic chair, which would use up almost the whole budget.
Another is a second monitor plus a nice keyboard and mouse.
Then there's a cheaper chair and a standing desk converter that sits on my current table.
Or finally, noise cancelling headphones and a good webcam for all my calls.
moshi_comment: If your back ever bothers you, the ergonomic chair is the best long-term investment, you'll use it every single hour. The second monitor is great for productivity, but comfort comes first. What's bugging you most right now?
The cheaper chair plus the standing desk converter gives you the most variety in posture for the money. The headphones and webcam only make sense if calls are a big part of your day.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm finally replacing my awful desk and I've got three in my basket, which one?
options: A solid oak desk from a secondhand shop, gorgeous and huge, but it weighs a ton and needs two people to move.
A cheap white flat pack desk that fits perfectly under the window, though it shakes a bit when I type.
An electric standing desk, quite pricey, with memory buttons for sitting and standing heights.
moshi_comment: The oak desk will last forever and secondhand is great value, as long as it fits through your door. The flat pack one is cheap, but a wobbly desk gets annoying every single day. If your budget allows, the standing desk gives you the most flexibility.
I'd skip the wobbly flat pack, you'll feel that shake on every call. Between the other two, it comes down to whether you'd actually stand. Do you get restless sitting all day?

option_sets.lead_in: My boss is offering three setups for remote staff and I have to pick by tomorrow.
options: Setup A gives me a monthly allowance for a coworking space, about twenty days a month.
Setup B is a one time budget of a thousand for home furniture and equipment.
With setup C I'd get a company laptop upgrade plus a fancy headset and webcam.
And setup D just pays a bit toward my internet and electricity bills every month.
moshi_comment: If your home has a good corner for working, the furniture budget pays off for years. The coworking allowance is the better deal if home is noisy or you feel isolated. The bill support is nice, but it's the least life changing of the four.

Setup B sounds strongest for most people, since a good chair and desk affect every working hour. Setup C only wins if your current laptop is genuinely holding you back. How's your current setup at home?

option_sets.lead_in: We're redoing the spare room and I can't settle on a plan for it.
options: Plan one makes it a full time office, desk, shelves, nice chair, nothing else in there.
Plan two keeps a sofa bed for guests and squeezes a small desk into the corner.
Plan three turns it into a shared office and hobby room, my desk on one side, a sewing table on the other.
moshi_comment: If guests only visit a couple of times a year, a full time office will make your workdays much nicer. The sofa bed plan keeps you flexible but you'll be cramped. The shared hobby room is lovely if the sewing table doesn't spill onto your desk.
How often do you actually host guests? If it's rare, plan one wins easily. Plan three is a sweet compromise if you love sewing, just add good storage so it doesn't turn into clutter.
